messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Okay, so i need about 650 m, the whole flight done in under 10 seconds, and landing under 15 ft/s.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 650 m (approximate, within 5%). The whole flight must finish in at most 10 s. Landing speed at most 15 ft/s, and 15 * 0.3048 = 4.57 m/s. Rail, wind, angle and site are not stated, so I assume a 1.5 m rail, 2 m/s wind, a vertical launch and sea level. One stage, since nothing asks for staging.
2. Feasibility: reaching 650 m with drag ignored and the whole impulse dumped at liftoff still needs sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 650) = 113 m/s upward. The coast from that speed back to zero takes 113 / 9.81 = 11.5 s, which is already over the 10 s cap, before a real burn, drag, or the descent. Altitude and flight time disagree with each other. I still want impulse and thrust for an F15, a G80 and an H128W so I can size the nearest rocket that does reach about 650 m and lands under 4.6 m/s, and then show how far the clock is from 10 s.

2. Feasibility: the F15 is 49.6 N*s at 14.5 N, the G80T is 135.6 N*s at 80.6 N, and the H128W is 177.8 N*s at 152.6 N. The vacuum round trip to 650 m and back is 2 * 11.5 = 23.0 s, so the 10 s cap is impossible on any of them, and a 4.57 m/s landing makes the flight longer still. The nearest useful rocket is one that still aims at about 650 m and lands under 4.57 m/s. The F15 only makes 14.5 N, which is soft if the airframe has to be heavy enough to keep the apogee from running away, and 135.6 / 49.6 = 2.73, so a G80T has nearly three times the impulse. I am checking a hotter F-class motor before freezing the draft.

2. Feasibility: the F67W is the motor I will fly. It gives 62.1 N*s at 73.3 N, burns for 0.85 s, weighs 0.080 kg and is single-use. The F40W carries more impulse, 78.1 N*s, but only 40.3 N and a 0.126 kg case. The G64W is 118 N*s, too much rocket for 650 m. The 10 s flight is still impossible. Falling from rest at 650 m takes sqrt(2 * 650 / 9.81) = 11.5 s even with no drag, and drag makes that fall slower, so the descent alone breaks the cap. I will aim the airframe at about 650 m and a landing under 4.57 m/s, and leave the time as the constraint that cannot be met.
3. Size: cardboard tube pi * 0.038 * 0.0008 * 0.48 * 700 = 0.032 kg. Three balsa fins 3 * 0.5 * (0.10 + 0.04) * 0.06 * 0.0032 * 160 = 0.0065 kg. Nose, mount, rings and chute 0.015 + 0.020 = 0.035 kg. Liftoff 0.032 + 0.0065 + 0.035 + 0.080 = 0.154 kg. Thrust-to-weight 73.3 / (0.154 * 9.81) = 48.5. Rail acceleration (73.3 - 0.154 * 9.81) / 0.154 = 466 m/s^2, and sqrt(2 * 466 * 1.5) = 37.4 m/s on the assumed 1.5 m rail. Propellant is 0.030 kg, so the chute sees 0.154 - 0.030 = 0.124 kg. For 4.0 m/s at Cd 0.8 the area is 2 * 0.124 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 4.0^2) = 0.155 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.155 / pi) = 0.444 m. A 0.50 m canopy keeps the landing under 4.57 m/s if the built mass is a bit high. The longest delay is 9 s, so ejection is at 0.85 + 9 = 9.85 s. The vacuum climb is 11.5 s, so the charge can be a little early, and 9 s is as late as this motor goes.
4. Draft: 38 mm cardboard tube 0.48 m long, 0.12 m ogive polystyrene nose, 0.032 m motor mount, F67W with a 9 s delay, three balsa fins (0.10 m root, 0.04 m tip, 0.06 m span, 0.045 m sweep) and a 0.50 m chute on motor ejection. Wind and rail were not stated, so the flight uses the 1.5 m rail and 2 m/s wind.

4. Check: the simulator gives 652.5 m. Against 650 m that is (652.5 - 650) / 650 = 0.385%, inside the 5% band. Landing is 4.2 m/s, under the 4.57 m/s limit. Rail exit 39.6 m/s, thrust-to-weight 45.9 and margin 1.36 cal all clear the gates. Flight time is 182.5 s, which misses the 10 s cap by a wide margin. Ejection is at 9.9 s, and 9.9 - 8.69 = 1.21 s after apogee, at 10.4 m/s. The landing still passes, so I am leaving the 9 s delay. Liftoff mass came out 0.163 kg, a bit over my 0.154 kg estimate, and the altitude landed on the target anyway.
5. Fix: no design change. Flight time 182.5 s cannot meet 10 s, since a drag-free fall from 652.5 m is sqrt(2 * 652.5 / 9.81) = 11.5 s.
6. Uncertainty: drag and chute Cd are model values, and the build will not weigh exactly 0.163 kg. The apogee is only 0.385% high, so a heavier build drops it out of the band quickly. The 1.36 cal margin is enough, but a 2 m/s wind will still weathercock a rocket that leaves the rail at 39.6 m/s and peaks at Mach 0.85. None of that uncertainty touches the time limit: the fall is too long.
messages.content:
Infeasible: the 10 second flight time cannot be met with an apogee of about 650 m and a landing under 4.57 m/s.
The simulated flight still takes 182.5 s, so the time limit fails. Closest safe rocket: F67W-9, 38 mm cardboard tube, 0.50 m chute, 652.5 m apogee, 4.2 m/s landing.
